Chapter 3: The Unconscious Dance of Attraction and Conflict
When two people come together, something fascinating happens beneath the surface. The imago—that collection of unconscious images and expectations we all carry—starts to shape not just the spark of attraction, but the entire course of the relationship.
At first, everything feels effortless, right? That early phase, where infatuation and idealization take center stage, is almost magical. You see the best in each other, and any differences just seem like charming quirks.
But as the relationship deepens, something shifts. The unconscious mind quietly begins searching for ways to heal old wounds. Suddenly, the very things you once loved about your partner might start to bother you. Maybe their independence, which you admired at first, now feels like they’re keeping you at arm’s length. Or that sense of humor you found so delightful? It might suddenly seem a bit dismissive—or even hurtful.
Now, here’s something to pay attention to: this shift doesn’t mean love is slipping away. In fact, it usually signals that the real work of the relationship is just beginning. The unconscious is nudging both partners to face and heal unfinished business from childhood.
The relationship becomes a place for growth—but only if you’re both willing to move beyond blame and defensiveness.
It’s at this stage that conflict often bubbles up. You might notice arguments starting to repeat themselves, but without much resolution. Both partners can end up feeling misunderstood or unappreciated. And let’s be honest, it’s tempting to think, “If only they would just change, everything would be better.” But that mindset tends to make the divide even wider.
So, what’s a better way forward? Try seeing conflict as a signal. It’s a clue that something deeper is going on. Instead of wondering how to change your partner, ask yourself, “What old wound is being touched here? And how can we work together to heal it?”
Shifting from blame to genuine curiosity can turn your relationship from a battleground into a space for real, mutual growth.
To help with this, it’s important to spot some common patterns that couples often fall into:
First, there’s the Pursuer-Distancer dynamic. One partner longs for closeness, while the other tends to pull away. The more one pursues, the more the other distances, and both end up feeling their fears are justified.
Then there’s the Criticize-Defend cycle. One person points out flaws, and the other gets defensive, which just leads to even more tension.
Finally, the Silent Withdrawal—where both partners retreat into themselves. This creates emotional distance and a growing sense of loneliness.
The thing is, these patterns aren’t unique to any one couple. They’re universal responses to unmet needs and old emotional wounds. But once you can name and understand these cycles, you can start to interrupt them—and create new, healthier ways of connecting.
